subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Rate of reaction and collision theory
Factors affecting rate (concentration, temperature, catalysts, surface area)

questions.q: Which of the following best defines the rate of a chemical reaction?
options: The change in amount of a reactant or product per unit time
The total mass of product formed in a reaction
The temperature at which a reaction begins
The number of reactants involved in a reaction
questions.explain: Rate of reaction measures how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed over time.

questions.q: If the rate of a reaction is followed by measuring the mass of gas lost, which unit is used for the mean rate?
options: g/s
cm³/s
mol/dm³
°C/s
questions.explain: When rate is measured by loss of mass, the mean rate is given in grams per second (g/s).

questions.q: According to collision theory, a reaction can only occur when particles collide with:
options: Sufficient energy and the correct orientation
Any amount of energy at all
A catalyst present in every collision
Exactly equal masses
questions.explain: Collision theory states particles must collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy) for a reaction to occur.

questions.q: What name is given to the minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react when they collide?
options: Activation energy
Kinetic energy
Thermal energy
Bond energy
questions.explain: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a successful (reactive) collision.

questions.q: Which of these changes would increase the rate of a reaction?
options: Increasing the temperature
Decreasing the concentration of a reactant
Using larger lumps instead of powder
Removing a catalyst
questions.explain: Increasing temperature raises the rate because particles collide more frequently and more energetically.

questions.q: What is a catalyst?
options: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up
A substance that is always used up in the reaction
A reactant that slows the reaction down
A product formed at the end of a reaction
questions.explain: A catalyst increases the rate of reaction but is not consumed, so it is not part of the overall equation.

questions.q: For a given mass of a solid reactant, which form reacts fastest with an acid?
options: A fine powder
A single large lump
A few medium lumps
The form makes no difference
questions.explain: A powder has the largest surface area to volume ratio, so there are more frequent collisions and a faster rate.

questions.q: Which symbol is used in an equation to show that a reaction is reversible?
questions.explain: The two half-arrows (⇌) show that the reaction can proceed in both the forward and backward directions.

questions.q: Why does increasing the concentration of a solution increase the rate of reaction?
options: There are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent
The particles gain more energy per collision
The activation energy of the reaction is lowered
The particles change into a different substance
questions.explain: Higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, increasing the frequency of collisions.

questions.q: Increasing the temperature speeds up a reaction for two reasons. Which pair is correct?
options: Particles move faster so collide more often, and more collisions have energy above the activation energy
Particles get bigger and the activation energy increases
Particles slow down but collide harder, and pressure falls
Concentration rises and the catalyst becomes more effective
questions.explain: Higher temperature increases both the frequency and the energy of collisions, so more collisions are successful.

questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It provides a different reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
It increases the activation energy of the reaction
It increases the concentration of the reactants
It raises the temperature of the reaction mixture
questions.explain: A catalyst offers an alternative route with lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

questions.q: Why does increasing the pressure of a reacting gas increase the rate of reaction?
options: The gas particles are closer together, so collisions are more frequent
The gas particles gain activation energy from the pressure
The gas particles become a liquid and react faster
The gas particles lose energy and slow down
questions.explain: Higher pressure pushes gas particles closer together, increasing the frequency of collisions.

questions.q: What is meant by a reaction being at dynamic equilibrium in a closed system?
options: The forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates
Both reactions have completely stopped
Only the forward reaction is taking place
All reactants have been converted to products
questions.explain: At equilibrium the forward and backward reactions continue but at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant.

questions.q: For a reversible reaction at equilibrium, what happens if the temperature is increased?
options: The equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction
The equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction
The reaction stops completely
The activation energy is removed
questions.explain: By Le Chatelier's principle, raising temperature favours the endothermic direction to counteract the change.

questions.q: For a reversible gas reaction at equilibrium, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with:
options: Fewer moles of gas
More moles of gas
The heavier molecules
No change in position
questions.explain: Increasing pressure moves the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules to reduce the pressure.

questions.q: On a graph of product formed against time, what does a steeper gradient (slope) indicate?
options: A faster rate of reaction
A slower rate of reaction
That the reaction has finished
That no product is being made
questions.explain: The gradient equals the rate, so a steeper line means product is forming more quickly.

questions.q: A reaction produces 24 cm³ of gas in 40 seconds. What is the mean rate of reaction?
options: 0.6 cm³/s
1.7 cm³/s
16 cm³/s
960 cm³/s
questions.explain: Mean rate = quantity of gas ÷ time = 24 ÷ 40 = 0.6 cm³/s.

questions.q: The forward reaction in a reversible system is exothermic. What happens to the yield of product if the temperature is increased?
options: The yield of product decreases
The yield of product increases
The yield of product stays exactly the same
The reaction becomes irreversible
questions.explain: Raising temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, reducing the yield of the exothermic product.

questions.q: In the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what is the effect on the amount of ammonia when the pressure is increased?
options: It increases, because the product side has fewer gas moles
It decreases, because the product side has more gas moles
It is unchanged, because pressure has no effect
It falls to zero, because the reaction reverses fully
questions.explain: The right side has 2 moles of gas versus 4 on the left, so higher pressure shifts equilibrium towards ammonia.

questions.q: A student compares magnesium ribbon and magnesium powder of equal mass reacting with the same acid. Which prediction is correct?
options: The powder reacts faster but produces the same total volume of gas
The ribbon reacts faster and produces more gas
The powder reacts slower and produces less gas
Both react at exactly the same rate
questions.explain: The powder's greater surface area speeds up the rate, but equal masses give the same total gas produced.

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; Rate & Extent of Change
